property_summary: For every caller and every target address k, when withdraw is invoked after the caller has a positive balance, the reference contract preserves balances[k] for other addresses (i.e., withdraw never clears another address's balance); the mutant can clear a balance even when the low-level send to a failing external callee fails because it ignores the send result and still zeroes balances[msg.sender].

For any caller and any target address k, calling withdraw preserves the balance of every address k != caller (the reference never clears other accounts' balances); the mutant can clear another address's balance when the low-level send to the caller fails and the contract still sets balances[msg.sender]=0, observable as balances[k] differing after withdraw.

For any caller and any target recipient address, when withdraw completes successfully the reference contract leaves balances[recipient] unchanged for all recipient addresses (it only transfers out the caller's balance when the external send succeeds), whereas the mutant that ignores the send result can clear balances[msg.sender] even when the external transfer to a failing recipient reverted — causing balances at some key to differ after withdraw.

After a withdraw call completes, the contract's balance is always zero in the reference (reentrancy-locked) implementation for any caller and deposited amount, but removing the lock allows a re-entrant attacker to drain additional funds so the contract balance can be non-zero after withdraw completes (violating the property) for some inputs.

For any caller and deposit amount, if the caller withdraws, the contract's balance remains equal to the contract's stored mapping balance for that caller (i.e., after withdraw completes the contract's balance decreased by exactly the withdrawn amount); removing the reentrancy lock allows a reentrant attacker to cause the contract's balance to be smaller than the mapping would have implied, violating this invariant for some inputs.

For any depositor and deposit amount, if that depositor calls withdraw, then after withdraw returns the contract's public balances[depositor] is zero (the reference clears the mapping for the caller even under reentrancy protection); removing the lock allows a reentrant attacker to cause balances[depositor] to be non-zero after withdraw returns for some inputs.

For any depositor and deposit amount, if an attacker contract (provided as the caller) deposits then calls withdraw, the reference implementation never allows the attacker to reenter and thereby increase its own balance after withdraw returns; i.e., after withdraw completes the contract's recorded balances[attacker] is zero (reference always clears to zero for all inputs), whereas removing the lock allows a reentrant attacker to make balances[attacker] > 0 for some inputs.

For any attacker address A and any deposit amount v>0, if A deposits v (via fallback) and then calls withdraw(), the reference contract C (with the lock) guarantees that address(c).balance equals 0 after withdraw completes when the attacker immediately withdrew all its recorded balance; the mutant without the lock can leave address(c).balance > 0 for some attacker implementations that reenter and steal funds, so the property is violated for some inputs and attacker behavior.

After a withdraw call that sends funds to a callee which may REVERT, the reference contract guarantees the caller's recorded balance remains unchanged when the external send fails (i.e., balances[caller] is NOT zero if the send reverted), while the mutant zeros the balance before checking send success, losing funds on failure.

For any caller and deposited amount, if an external send from withdraw to the caller reverts, the reference contract preserves the caller's recorded balance (balances[caller] remains equal to the deposited amount) whereas the mutant zeroes the balance before checking send success and thus loses the recorded balance on a reverting send.

If withdraw() is called and the external transfer to the recipient reverts, the reference contract preserves the caller's recorded balance (balances[caller] stays equal to the deposited amount), whereas the mutant zeros the balance before checking the send result and thus would set balances[caller] to 0 when the send fails.

If the external call inside withdraw() reverts, the correct contract preserves the caller's recorded balance (balances[caller] stays equal to their deposit) while the mutant that zeroes the balance before checking the send result will make balances[caller] become zero; we express this by calling withdraw() where the recipient is a contract that always reverts and asserting balances[attacker] remains deposit in the correct contract (the mutant will fail for some fuzzed deposit amounts).

For any depositor and deposit amount, if withdraw() is called and the external send to msg.sender succeeds, the depositor's recorded balance becomes zero afterwards (funds actually transferred); the mutant that zeroes the balance before checking send success can cause divergence when the external send fails, but we target the success-path rule so the reference always zeros balance on successful send while the mutant may differ for some inputs.
